title: One-Dimensional Kronig-Penney Model
short_intro: The one-dimensional Kronig-Penney model is a simplified quantum mechanical treatment of an electron moving in a periodic rectangular potential well. It explains the emergence of energy bands and forbidden gaps in crystalline solids.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of periodic potentials, qualitative energy band formation, and Bloch theorem statement.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical derivation of the dispersion relation, evaluation of the P-function, effective mass, and classification of conductors, insulators, and semiconductors.

prerequisites: Quantum tunneling and wave packet behavior

concept_notes.heading: Periodic Potential Model
bullets: The potential energy V(x) satisfies the periodicity condition V(x + a) = V(x), where a is the lattice constant.
In the Kronig-Penney model, this potential is approximated as an infinite array of rectangular potential barriers of height V<sub>0</sub> and width b, separated by wells of width a - b.
As V<sub>0</sub> approaches infinity and b approaches zero such that their product V<sub>0</sub>ba remains finite, the potential reduces to a series of Dirac delta functions.

concept_notes.heading: Bloch's Theorem
bullets: Bloch's theorem states that the wavefunction psi(x) of an electron in a periodic potential is modulated by a plane wave.
Mathematically, psi(x) = exp(ikx) u<sub>k</sub>(x), where u<sub>k</sub>(x) has the periodicity of the lattice: u<sub>k</sub>(x + a) = u<sub>k</sub>(x).
The parameter k is the crystal momentum wavevector, which determines the translational symmetry state of the electron.

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Energy Bands and Forbidden Gaps
bullets: Matching the wavefunctions and their derivatives at the boundaries leads to a transcendental equation involving the energy E.
Since the left-hand side of the Kronig-Penney condition must lie between -1 and +1 for real solutions of k to exist, allowed energy bands are formed.
Values of energy for which the condition is violated correspond to forbidden energy gaps (band gaps).

concept_notes.heading: Effective Mass of an Electron
bullets: An electron moving through a periodic lattice experiences internal forces from the ion cores, altering its response to external electric and magnetic fields.
The effective mass m* is defined via the curvature of the E-k dispersion relation: m* = h_bar<sup>2</sup> / (d<sup>2</sup>E / dk<sup>2</sup>).
Near the Brillouin zone boundary, d<sup>2</sup>E / dk<sup>2</sup> can become negative, resulting in a negative effective mass.

derivations.title: Kronig-Penney Dispersion Relation Derivation
derivations.conditions: One-dimensional rectangular potential barrier of width b and height V<sub>0</sub>, with well width a - b.
steps: Write the time-independent Schrödinger equation for Region I (0 < x < a-b, V=0) and Region II (-b < x < 0, V=V<sub>0</sub>).

Assume solutions using Bloch theorem: psi<sub>I</sub>(x) = A exp(i alpha x) + B exp(-i alpha x) and psi<sub>II</sub>(x) = C exp(beta x) + D exp(-beta x), where alpha<sup>2</sup> = 2mE/h_bar<sup>2</sup> and beta<sup>2</sup> = 2m(V<sub>0</sub> - E)/h_bar<sup>2</sup>.
Apply continuity conditions for the wavefunctions and their first derivatives at x = 0 and x = a - b.
Set the determinant of the resulting homogeneous system of linear equations for coefficients A, B, C, D to zero.
Take the limit V<sub>0</sub> -> infinity and b -> 0 such that (m V<sub>0</sub> b a) / h_bar<sup>2</sup> = P (scattering strength).

derivations.title: Number of Allowed States per Band
derivations.conditions: A crystal lattice containing N unit cells with periodic boundary conditions.
steps: Apply Born-Karman periodic boundary conditions over a crystal of length L = Na: psi(x + L) = psi(x).
This implies exp(ikL) = 1, leading to k = (2\pi / L) n, where n is an integer.
The interval of k in the first Brillouin zone is from -\pi/a to \pi/a, spanning a total range of 2\pi/a.
Divide the total k-space range by the spacing between allowed k states: \Delta k = 2\pi / L = 2\pi / (Na).
Total number of k-states = (2\pi/a) / (2\pi/Na) = N. Considering two electrons per state due to spin, each band accommodates 2N electrons.
derivations.result: Each energy band contains exactly 2N allowed states, where N is the number of unit cells.

graphs_and_experiments.title: E versus k Dispersion Curve (Reduced Zone Scheme)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of energy E vertically against crystal momentum k horizontally, showing parabolic segments folded into the first Brillouin zone (-pi/a to pi/a) with band gaps opening up at the zone boundaries.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Discontinuities in energy appear at k = \pm n\pi/a, representing the forbidden energy gaps caused by Bragg reflection of electron waves from the lattice planes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in PGT multiple-choice questions regarding band gap locations and zone boundaries.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Graphical Solution of Kronig-Penney Condition
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of the function f(alpha a) = (P sin(alpha a) / alpha a) + cos(alpha a) versus alpha a, along with horizontal lines drawn at +1 and -1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Allowed energy bands correspond to regions where the function curve lies strictly between +1 and -1. Intersections define the edges of allowed and forbidden bands.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to explain why certain energy ranges yield real values of crystal momentum k.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Effective Mass m* versus Wavevector k
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing m* starting near the band bottom as positive, increasing towards the band edge, diverging, and becoming negative near the top of the energy band.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that electrons near the top of an energy band respond to external forces with an effective negative mass, corresponding to hole conduction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in advanced PGT numericals and conceptual questions on semiconductor transport.

solved_numericals.question: What is the periodicity condition of the potential energy V(x) in a one-dimensional crystal lattice with lattice parameter a?
solution_steps: Recall the definition of a periodic crystal lattice.
The potential experienced by an electron must reflect the periodic arrangement of positive ion cores.
Therefore, V(x) must be invariant under a translation by any lattice vector R = na.

solved_numericals.question: In the limiting case where the scattering power P -> 0, what does the Kronig-Penney dispersion relation reduce to?
solution_steps: Start with the Kronig-Penney equation: (P sin(alpha a) / alpha a) + cos(alpha a) = cos(ka).
Set P = 0, which eliminates the first term on the left-hand side.
This simplifies the expression to cos(alpha a) = cos(ka).
Therefore, alpha = k, substituting alpha yields E = h_bar^2 k^2 / 2m.
solved_numericals.answer: Free electron energy relation: E = \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the width of the first allowed energy band for alpha a -> 0 when P is very large, given lattice constant a = 0.3 nm.
solution_steps: For small alpha a, the Kronig-Penney relation simplifies near the band edge.
Using P sin(alpha a) / alpha a + cos(alpha a) = 1 for the lower band edge when alpha a is small.
Approximating sin(alpha a) / alpha a \approx 1 and cos(alpha a) \approx 1 - (alpha a)^2 / 2.
Solving for alpha gives the lowest allowed energy value corresponding to the bottom of the band.
solved_numericals.answer: Energy corresponds to discrete quantized levels of a particle in a box as P -> \infty

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The potential is strictly one-dimensional, ignoring transverse components of electron motion. Limitation: Real crystals are three-dimensional, requiring reciprocal lattice vectors in three dimensions.
Assumption: The ion core potential is represented by rectangular or delta-function barriers. Limitation: Real potentials are smooth, Coulombic, and dynamic due to lattice vibrations (phonons).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Forbidden energy gaps mean electrons cannot exist anywhere inside the crystal at those energies.
common_misconceptions.correct: Forbidden gaps mean no traveling wave solutions with real wavevector k exist within the crystal for those specific energy values.
common_misconceptions.why: Wavefunctions at forbidden energies correspond to complex wavevectors, leading to exponentially decaying evanescent waves.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bloch electrons have the same mass as free electrons.
common_misconceptions.correct: Bloch electrons move through a periodic lattice and possess an effective mass m* that can be different from m and even negative.
common_misconceptions.why: The periodic interaction with the lattice modifies the kinematic response of the electron to external forces.

quick_revision: The Kronig-Penney model solves the 1D Schrödinger equation for a periodic rectangular well potential to explain energy bands.
Bloch's theorem states that wavefunctions in a periodic potential are plane waves modulated by a lattice-periodic function.
The consistency equation (P sin(alpha a)/alpha a) + cos(alpha a) = cos(ka) dictates allowed and forbidden energy bands.
Effective mass m* accounts for internal lattice forces and is determined by the curvature of the E-k dispersion curve.
